questions.q: Why does the query use COUNT(DISTINCT soh.SalesOrderID) instead of COUNT(*) for OrderCount?
options: Joining to SalesOrderDetail repeats each SalesOrderID once per line item, so COUNT(*) would count line items rather than orders
COUNT(*) is not valid T-SQL syntax
SalesOrderID can contain NULL values that COUNT(*) would skip
DISTINCT is required any time GROUP BY is used
questions.explain: Because the FROM starts at SalesOrderDetail, an order with three line items appears three times, so counting distinct order IDs is needed to get a true order count.

questions.explain: DATEPART(QUARTER, ...) gives the current quarter number, which the formula converts to that quarter's starting month, then DATEFROMPARTS assembles day 1 of that month.

questions.q: Why does the WHERE clause use >= on the start date and < on the end date rather than <=?
options: It makes the query run faster regardless of correctness
T-SQL does not support the <= operator on date columns
It is required whenever COUNT(DISTINCT ...) appears in the SELECT list
It creates a half-open range that avoids double-counting a boundary date between quarters
questions.explain: Using >= on the start and < on the end means a date exactly on the next quarter's first day is correctly excluded rather than counted in both ranges.

questions.q: Why does the query's FROM clause start at Sales.SalesOrderDetail rather than Sales.SalesOrderHeader?
options: Production.Product can only be joined directly to SalesOrderDetail
LineTotal, the amount being summed, lives on SalesOrderDetail, and starting there avoids double-counting order-level totals
SQL Server requires FROM to start with the table listed first alphabetically
SalesOrderHeader does not have a TerritoryID column
questions.explain: This matches the Lesson 2 plan: starting from the table holding the number you're aggregating prevents summing an order's total once per line item.

questions.q: What governs which columns must appear in this query's GROUP BY clause?
options: Only columns from the first table listed in FROM need to be grouped
Aggregate functions like SUM must also be listed in GROUP BY
Every column in SELECT that isn't wrapped in an aggregate function (here, st.Name and p.ProductLine) must appear in GROUP BY
GROUP BY must list every column referenced anywhere in the query
questions.explain: This is the standard GROUP BY rule: non-aggregated SELECT columns must be part of the grouping, which is why st.Name and p.ProductLine both appear in GROUP BY.
